phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s], as in English 'stone'; Old Norse initial s is plain, never voiced.
Short high back rounded [u], as in English 'put', held brief — Old Norse short u, not the long ú.
The long (geminate) stop [tː] straddling the two syllables, held audibly as in modern Icelandic and Italian 'notte'.
Second short high back rounded [u], identical to the first — the name keeps its vowel uniform.
Velar nasal plus stop [ŋɡ] closing on a syllabic trill [r̩] — the nominative ending -r, sounded as a true r, not swallowed.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SOOT-toongr' — two beats, the first stressed, the double t held a fraction long in the middle, and the final -r trilled as a syllable of its own, as in Icelandic Suttungur.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Suttungr, son of the giant Gillingr, brother of Baugi and father of Gunnlöð; the name is attested only for this giant.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛋᚢᛏᛏᚢᚾᚴᚱ (normalized suttunkr), the Viking-Age runic rendering — the short-twig row writes t and d alike, and ᚴ covers both k and g.

kin.label: Manuscript Latin
kin.form: Suttungr, unchanged — the Icelandic codices of the Poetic and Prose Edda write the name in plain Latin bookhand.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Suttungur, with the regular modern nominative ending -ur replacing medieval -r.

pronunciation.note: Suttungr is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The figure's centrality to the mead myth vastly outruns his name's orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Giant, Guardian of Mead
domains.subtitle: The Jötunn Who Hoarded Poetry in the Mountain
domains.lead: Suttungr, son of Gillingr and brother of Baugi, is the giant who came to own the mead of poetry — the blood of wise Kvasir, brewed by the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar and yielded up as ransom for their lives. He stored it in the mountain Hnitbjörg, in the three vats Óðrerir, Boðn, and Són, and set his own daughter Gunnlöð to guard it. His whole mythology is the story of that hoard and its loss: Óðinn came disguised as the wanderer Bölverkr, drilled through the rock, lay three nights with Gunnlöð, drank the vats dry, and flew home as an eagle with Suttungr's wings one beat behind him. From that flight, every poet drinks.

cards.name: The Mead of Poetry
cards.desc: Kvasir's blood mixed with honey — the drink that makes a man a poet or a scholar, hoarded by Suttungr in three vats deep inside the mountain.

cards.name: Hnitbjörg
cards.desc: The 'clashing rocks' or beating-rocks where Suttungr set his treasure — the mountain stronghold no hand could enter until an auger made a door.

cards.name: Gunnlöð on the Golden Seat
cards.desc: The daughter set to guard the vats, who gave Óðinn three nights and three drinks — and wept when the price of the mead was paid in a false oath.

cards.name: The Auger Rati
cards.desc: The drill-bit whose mouth gnawed through the mountain — Óðinn holding the shaft, Baugi boring, and a snake slipping through the hole at the end.

symbols.name: The vats Óðrerir, Boðn, and Són
symbols.meaning: The three vessels of the poetry-mead — 'mind-stirrer', 'offering', and 'atonement' — emptied in three drinks

symbols.name: Hnitbjörg
symbols.meaning: The mountain vault of the mead — treasure sealed in stone, poetry kept from the world

symbols.name: The auger Rati
symbols.meaning: The boring tool that made the snake-road into the rock — the slender breach through which all poetry escaped

symbols.name: The eagle form
symbols.meaning: Óðinn's flight with the mead, pursued by Suttungr in eagle shape — the chase every kenning remembers

symbols.name: The skerry at flood
symbols.meaning: The tide-washed rock where Suttungr stranded the dwarf-murderers until they paid him the mead — the ransom that made him poetry's gaoler

mythology.lead: Suttungr's dossier is one continuous story told in two keys: Snorri's Skáldskaparmál narrates the mead's making, hoarding, and theft as prose history, while Hávamál lets Óðinn himself remember it in verse — a man confessing, between counsels, to seduction, perjury, and grand larceny. Between them stands the corpus's fullest portrait of a giant who was never the fool of the story.

myths.title: How Suttungr Won the Mead
myths.text:
When the Æsir and the Vanir made peace, they sealed the truce by spitting into a vat, and from the spittle they fashioned a man, Kvasir, wisest of all beings — no question was asked him he could not answer. He travelled the world teaching wisdom, until the dwarfs Fjalar and Galar killed him in private, drained his blood into two vats and a kettle named Óðrerir, Boðn, and Són, and mixed it with honey: that is the mead of poetry, of which whoever drinks becomes a skald or a sage.

The dwarfs' violence did not end there. They invited the giant Gillingr to row with them and capsized the boat — Gillingr, who could not swim, drowned — and when his wife wept at the news, Galar dropped a millstone on her head as she passed under the lintel. Then Suttungr, Gillingr's son, came for the reckoning. He seized the dwarfs, carried them out to sea, and stranded them on a skerry that the tide would cover. They begged for their lives and offered the precious mead as ransom, and Suttungr accepted: blood-guilt paid in blood-brew. He carried the mead home, stored it in the mountain called Hnitbjörg, and set his daughter Gunnlöð to watch over it. This is why poetry is called Kvasir's blood, the dwarfs' drink — and Suttungr's mead.

myths.title: Bölverkr at the Mountain
myths.text:
Óðinn set out to take the mead, and he did not take it by force. Disguised as a wanderer who named himself Bölverkr — 'evil-doer', the one honest name in the whole affair — he came upon nine slaves mowing hay for Baugi, Suttungr's brother, sharpened their scythes on a whetstone, and let them kill each other in the quarrel over it. Then he offered Baugi to do nine men's work for the summer, for one wage: a drink of Suttungr's mead. Baugi warned that he had no say over his brother's treasure but agreed to try.

When the summer was done, Suttungr flatly refused the bargain. Bölverkr then produced the auger called Rati and had Baugi bore through the mountain to the mead-chamber; when Baugi claimed the hole went through, Bölverkr blew into it and chips flew back in his face — the first tunnel was a cheat — and at the second boring the chips flew inward. Then Bölverkr turned himself into a snake, wriggled into the auger-hole, and Baugi stabbed after him with the drill and missed. Inside, he came to Gunnlöð, lay with her for three nights, and she granted him three drinks of the mead: at the first he emptied Óðrerir, at the second Boðn, at the third Són — the whole hoard. Then he took eagle shape and flew, and Suttungr, taking eagle shape himself, flew after him.

myths.title: The Eagle Chase and the Rhymester's Share
myths.text:
The Æsir saw Óðinn's flight coming and set out vats in the court of Ásgarðr, and when he came in over the wall with Suttungr's eagle at his tail-feathers, he spewed the mead up into the vessels. But Suttungr had come so close that Óðinn, in his fear, sent some of the mead out backwards — and that portion no one bothered to gather: it was left for anyone who wanted it, and it is called the rhymester's share, the bad poet's portion. The good mead Óðinn gives to the Æsir and to those men who know how to compose.

Hávamál lets the god tell his own version, and it is less heroic. He boasts that he got little by silence in Suttungr's hall and spoke many words to his advantage; he records that Gunnlöð gave him a drink of the precious mead from her golden seat, and that the reward he paid her was poor — 'her whole heart, her sorrowful spirit'; he remembers letting Rati's mouth gnaw the rock and the paths of the giants standing over and under him. And he confesses the cost to others: the frost-giants came to Hár's hall asking after Bölverkr, whether he had reached the gods or Suttungr had slain him — and Óðinn, the poem says, had sworn a ring-oath, and who now can trust his oaths? He had robbed Suttungr of his mead and made Gunnlöð weep. The verses that frame the memory call the whole episode a drunken night at wise Fjalar's, from which a man comes home wiser — and the forgetfulness-heron broods over the drink of every mortal.

myths.title: The Giant Poetry Is Named After
myths.text:
Suttungr lost the treasure and kept the name. Skáldskaparmál's catalogue of kennings for poetry runs through his story at every turn: verse is the mead of Suttungr, the find of Óðinn, the drink of the dwarfs, the liquid of Óðrerir, the freight of the eagle, Gunnlöð's lost wealth. No other jötunn is so woven into the language of the skalds' own craft — every poet who named his art named its former owner.

The þulur, the metrical name-lists preserved with the Edda, hold him among the jǫtna heiti, the giants' names, in the company of his mountain-kin — a gaoler catalogued with the figures he belongs to. And the handbooks note the strangeness of his standing: Suttungr is called wise, keeps a hall the god himself praises, and bargains in good faith at every step of the story — a giant whose only crime was to own what a god decided to steal.

lore.syncretism: Suttungr's closest kin are inside the corpus itself. The mead myth belongs to the great northern pattern of the coveted treasure prised from giant-keepers: Þórr winning the mile-wide brewing cauldron from Hymir so that Ægir can brew for the gods is the same plot in beer rather than poetry, and Lindow reads the two tales as sibling statements about how culture's goods are obtained — never made at home, always taken across the boundary. Cross-culturally, the comparativists' dossier is older and larger: Dumézil and the Indo-European school long paired Óðinn's mead-theft with the Indic myths of soma won by the eagle — the bird that carries the intoxicating draught of inspiration down to the gods — and the parallel is genuinely striking, a divine bird, a guarded liquor, a theft that founds an art. Current handbooks keep the comparison but drop the certainty: Simek and Orchard treat Suttungr as a figure wholly of the mead complex, with no cult, no place-name, and no etymology solid enough to build on. What can be said cleanly is that no other northern giant stands so exactly at the hinge of loss and gift — the one who held poetry so that a god could steal it, and whose name every kenning for verse goes on paying.
lore.culturalLegacy: Suttungr's afterlife is the afterlife of the mead itself: every retelling of Norse poetry's origin, from the Kearys' Victorian 'Heroes of Asgard' onward, replays the auger-hole, the golden seat, and the two eagles over the wall of Ásgarðr. The romantics loved Gunnlöð and made Suttungr a brooding proprietor; the skaldic scholars made him something rarer, a mnemonic fixed point — because 'Suttungr's mead' stayed a living kenning, his name travelled inside every stanza that called verse by its owner's title. In modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice he is remembered, with some sympathy, at the edge of sumbel and skaldic rites as the giant from whom inspiration was taken, and the 'rhymester's share' — the mead spilt backwards in the chase — survives as the tradition's own dry name for bad verse. As a personal name he never entered the living Scandinavian stock; his immortality is entirely literary, and it is complete.
lore.extendedMeditation: Suttungr is the rare giant who loses nothing through his own fault. He avenged his father lawfully, took ransom in the manner of his world, stored his treasure in stone, set his own child as its guard, and refused a bargain he had every right to refuse. Then a god lied to his brother, seduced his daughter, and emptied his mountain — and the tradition tells the story as a triumph, and names the product after the victim. The myth knows what it is doing: Hávamál makes Óðinn himself recite the perjury, and the kennings keep Suttungr's name on the mead as if to balance the account. Poetry, the North seems to say, is not a thing that can be owned — but it can be hoarded, and the difference between the giant's vault and the god's gift is only the auger-hole between them. Every verse ever drunk from the vats of Óðrerir, Boðn, and Són is poured, in the end, from Suttungr's loss.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Suttungr — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛋᚢᛏᛏᚢᚾᚴᚱ (normalized suttunkr, the sixteen-rune row writing t and d alike and covering both k and g with ᚴ). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was available to anyone decades ago: suttungr.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Suttungr is a wholly textual giant: no runestone invokes him, no votive deposit names him, and no Viking-Age image can be securely identified with his story. His attestation hangs on the manuscript witnesses of the mead myth — the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda for Hávamál's account, and the Codex Regius of Snorri's Edda with its fellow codices for Skáldskaparmál's continuous narrative. The story's pictorial life begins only in the early modern North: the eighteenth-century Icelandic paper manuscripts of the Edda (SÁM 66 and the Melsteð Edda) illustrate the myth with woodcut-style scenes — Óðinn as an eagle above the Æsir's waiting vats, Suttungr's eagle behind him — proof of the tale's hold on post-medieval readers, not of older iconography. Claims that figures on the Gotland picture stones depict the mead of poetry remain interpretive and are not accepted as secure identifications; the stone record is silent, and the word-hoard of the skalds — the kennings that kept 'Suttungr's mead' current for centuries — is the only true monument.
